title: Smash the Two Heaviest
statement:
You have a pile of rocks with positive integer weights stones. Repeat this step while at least two rocks are left: take the two heaviest rocks, with weights x ≤ y, and smash them together.

  • If x == y, both rocks are destroyed.
  • Otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one goes back on the pile with weight y − x.

Return the weight of the rock left at the end, or 0 if none is left.

examples.why: 10 and 4 leave 6, which is again the heaviest. Then 6 and 3 leave 3, and 3 and 2 leave 1. Pairing the sorted list once, (10, 4) then (3, 2), would give 5.
Equal rocks destroy each other. The two 6s vanish, then the two 2s, and nothing is left.
A single rock is never smashed.

hints: Each step needs the two largest values, and then one new value may join the pile. Sorting once at the start is not enough. Why?
The leftover y − x can be heavier than everything else, or lighter. You need a structure that gives you the current maximum after every insert.
Use a max-heap. Pop two, push the difference if it is not zero, and repeat until at most one rock is left.

explain.intuition:
This is a direct simulation, and the only question is how to find the two heaviest rocks quickly every time. The pile changes after each smash: a new rock of weight y − x may join it, and it can land anywhere in the order. A sorted array would need an O(n) insert to stay sorted. A max-heap gives the heaviest rock in O(log n) and takes the leftover back in O(log n).

Python's heapq is a min-heap only. The standard trick is to store negated weights: the heaviest rock, say 10, becomes -10, the smallest number in the heap, so it sits on top. Negate again when you read it. In TypeScript, a heap class with the comparison flipped (a[p] >= a[i]) is a max-heap directly. Each smash removes at least one rock, so there are at most n − 1 rounds.
steps: Put all weights into a max-heap (in Python: heap = [-s for s in stones], then heapify).
While the heap holds at least two rocks: pop y (heaviest), then pop x.
At the end return the remaining weight, or 0 if the heap is empty.
pitfalls: Sorting once and smashing neighbours in pairs. The leftover must compete again: on example 1 that shortcut answers 5 instead of 1.
In Python, forgetting to negate the value back, or pushing y − x without negating it. The heap then mixes positive and negative weights and pops the wrong rock.
Reading the top of the heap at the end without checking that it is empty. When every rock is destroyed, as in example 2, the answer is 0, and heap[0] throws in Python.

solutions.title: Re-sort after every smash
solutions.idea: Sort the pile, smash the two heaviest, put the leftover back, sort again.

solutions.title: Max-heap simulation
solutions.idea: Keep the rocks in a max-heap. Pop two, push the difference if it is positive.

followups: Weights are at most 1000. Can you avoid the heap with a counting array, and when is that faster?
Now you may choose any two rocks at each step. What is the smallest possible final weight? (It becomes a subset-sum problem.)
